UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                     )
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                           )                         Docket No. ER26-2249-000
                                                     )                                    ER26-2249-001
                                                     )                                    ER26-2249-002
                                                     )


             COMMENTS OF OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY

        Pursuant to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” or “Commission”)

notice in the above-captioned proceeding,1 Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E”)

respectfully submits these comments in response to the September 18, 2026 Deficiency Response

filed by Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”).2 SPP’s Deficiency Response fails to remedy the

deficiencies highlighted by the Commission; the concerns raised by the SPP Market Monitoring

Unit (“MMU”); the issues raised in the Transmission Owners’ Protest (“TO Protest”);3 and the

new complications raised by the Executive Order issued in August 2026, which prohibits certain

acquisitions, imports, transfers, or installations of foreign-produced bulk-power system electric

equipment (the “EO”).4 Indeed, rather than curing the deficiencies identified by the Commission

or stakeholders, SPP’s Deficiency Response confirms that SPP seeks Commission approval of a



1
 Combined Notice of Filings, Docket No. ER26-2249-000 (Sept. 18, 2026). On April 17, 2026, as amended on May
6, 2026, Southwest Power Pool, Inc. submitted revisions to its Open Access Transmission Tariff to (1) create a Peak
Demand Assessment, which compares pre-season qualified capacity to actual, weather-normalized Peak Demand; and
(2) incorporate demand response into SPP’s operations and resource adequacy framework (“SPP Proposal” or
“Proposal”). On August 19, 2026, the Commission issued a Deficiency Notice to SPP.
2
  Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Response to Deficiency Notice, Docket No. ER26-2249-000 (filed Sept. 18, 2026)
(“Deficiency Response”).
3
 Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Protest of Transmission Owner Group, Docket No. ER26-2249-000 (filed May 27,
2026) (“TO Protest”). OG&E was a signatory to the TO Protest.
4
 Executive Order 14421, Declaring a National Emergency to Secure the United States Bulk-Power System, 91 Fed.
Reg. 55,995 (Aug. 31, 2026) (“EO”).

                                                         1
 financially binding compliance regime while leaving material terms governing compliance

unresolved. SPP would defer those outcome-determinative provisions to future compliance filings,

stakeholder processes, and business practices, thereby asking the Commission to authorize binding

obligations before the governing framework is complete or subject to meaningful review. Such a

result would leave entities unable to react in a timely manner, undermining affordability and

compliance efforts.

       SPP’s Deficiency Response confirms that core elements of its Proposal remain harmful to

the market, unnecessary, and either undefined or buried in Business Practice manuals. More

fundamentally, under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), SPP cannot meet its burden

of proof that its Proposal is just and reasonable, because the record lacks meaningful evidence that

the Proposal even addresses an actual reliability problem, or key details on how it would do so.

Instead, SPP asks the Commission to authorize significant compliance obligations and deficiency-

payment exposure based largely on speculative forecasting assumptions and reliability modeling

that stakeholders have been unable to independently evaluate.

       Although SPP shifted its requested effective date from January 1, 2027 to June 1, 2027,

this modest delay does not cure the Proposal’s fundamental deficiencies or afford Load

Responsible Entities (“LREs”) adequate time to comply. The current state of SPP’s Proposal,

together with the issues raised in the Deficiency Notice, deepens the regulatory uncertainty

surrounding what obligations may be imminently imposed on OG&E. Specifically, SPP’s Proposal

leaves OG&E unable to determine with reasonable certainty what Demand Response (“DR”)

resources will qualify, how those DR resources will be accredited, what demand reductions will

ultimately count (or be significantly reduced) toward compliance, or what level of deficiency-

payment exposure may result.



                                                 2
            These uncertainties are compounded by the EO, which fundamentally changes the

landscape for procuring additional generation and further erodes the basis for SPP’s Proposal. The

EO calls into question the viability of alternatives that OG&E was seeking to manage the risks

created by SPP’s Proposal.5 These unresolved regulatory and supply-chain issues make it

unreasonable to require OG&E to make immediate, financially significant planning and

investment decisions based on a framework that remains materially undefined. The EO does not

merely increase cost or complexity; it forecloses or delays access to categories of equipment

necessary to develop replacement capacity while the governing restrictions and implementing rules

remain unsettled. Even if OG&E were to begin procurement immediately, it could not reasonably

complete equipment selection, regulatory approvals, contracting, construction, testing, and

commercial operation by the proposed deadline. The resulting timing problem is not one of

preference or administrative convenience; it is a practical impossibility created by federal

restrictions,6 uncertain implementing rules,7 and unavoidable project-development lead times.8

           If the Commission does not deny SPP’s filing, including for the reasons set forth in the

MMU Protest and the TO Protest, it should, at minimum, defer application of SPP’s Proposal and

the financially binding Peak Demand Assessment (“PDA”) to OG&E by five years, until the 2033




5
  Such alternatives are among the only options available to OG&E to manage the risks created by the Proposal.
Moreover, compliance with the SPP Proposal as proposed essentially forces utilities to procure those resources that
may be available, versus what may otherwise be efficient in terms of customer cost and resource accreditation. An
accelerated deadline can force procurement based on near-term availability, to the detriment of procurement based on
lowest reasonable cost, operational fit, reliability contribution, or long-term customer value.
6
    See SPP Proposal; supra n.4.
7
  In addition to the uncertainty surrounding this proceeding and its potential implementation timeline, the EO provides
that the Department of Energy has until December 24, 2026 to publish formal rules implementing the order.
8
  See Kavya Balaraman, US power companies scramble to secure equipment as surging data center demand strains
supplies, REUTERS (July 9, 2026), available at https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/us-power-companies-
scramble-secure-equipment-surging-data-center-demand-strains-2026-07-09/.

                                                          3
 Summer Season. Compliance with SPP’s Proposal requires both time and certainty to ensure that

customers only bear the lowest, reasonable costs of service. Neither exists here.

           I.       COMMENTS

                       A. SPP’s Response Does Not Cure the Deficiencies Identified in the TO
                          Protest

           As the TO Protest demonstrated, SPP’s Proposal is deficient for many reasons, and SPP’s

Deficiency Response fails to remedy those deficiencies.

                             i.    SPP’s Proposal Lacks Adequate Evidentiary Support

           SPP has not provided adequate evidentiary support to justify the need to impose a PDA on

the proposed schedule. Accordingly, under Section 205 of the FPA, SPP has not demonstrated that

the proposed penalty construct is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory. The

Commission may not presume the existence of the conduct SPP seeks to deter: that LREs

systematically under-forecast load. LREs are already subject to the Planning Reserve Margin

(“PRM”) that SPP sets under Attachment AA of its Tariff.9 SPP’s stance that its Proposal is

necessary to resolve resource sufficiency is undercut by its own PRM administration under its

FERC-approved tariff. Because the PDA would impose material financial consequences, the

Commission should require SPP to establish both the existence of the asserted problem and a

rational connection between the record evidence and the remedy proposed, before authorizing the

new penalty construct.

           SPP’s reliability analysis from the Proposal docket projects that, with a 2028

implementation date and no cap on load modifiers, the SPP footprint could experience 9.5 days of

EEA1/EEA2 declarations in the summer, 2.5 days in the winter, 0.4 to 0.6 days of firm load shed




9
    SPP Tariff, Attach. AA, § 4.

                                                   4
 in both seasons, and a potential reduction of 1.5 million MWh (2 percent) of available

maintenance.10 That analysis, however, assumes a 2028 implementation date with no cap on load

modifiers and does not assess realistic interim alternatives.

           SPP members have not been given access to the model underlying SPP’s reliability

projections and therefore cannot fully assess its reasonableness or accuracy. Without access to the

model, stakeholders have had no meaningful opportunity to examine the assumptions, inputs,

sensitivities, or methodology or to independently validate its results. The Commission should not

approve a sweeping redesign of the resource adequacy framework based on modeling that affected

stakeholders have been unable to review, particularly when SPP’s failure to provide access to the

model itself raises substantial questions about the need for such reform or the reliability of the

conclusions drawn from it.

           Based on the materials SPP did provide its working groups, it appears that SPP constructed

an extreme hypothetical scenario, inconsistent with any recent or historical pattern, designed to

maximize reliability concerns rather than evaluate realistic outcomes.11 An appropriately phased

implementation (with adequate evidentiary support and transitional reliability protections) could

address SPP’s stated reliability concerns, without rushing LREs into financially binding

compliance before they can complete the required regulatory, contractual, and procurement steps.




10
     Deficiency Response at 6.
11
  For example, it appears SPP’s analysis removed generators from its model and replaced them with demand response,
and applied a response percentage of 40-60%—an extreme scenario. See Deficiency Response at 6; see also SPP,
RR703 Demand Response and LRE Peak Demand Assessment Policy Framework at 7 (Jan. 2026). SPP also assumed
4,304 MW of demand response by Summer 2027. Id. However, SPP’s most recent Resource Adequacy report shows
that LREs claimed a total of 1,857 MW of demand response resources this year. See SPP, Resource Adequacy Report:
East Balancing Authority Area, 2026 Summer Season at 6 (June 15, 2026). Growth to 4,304 MW by Summer 2027—
more than double the known amount of demand response during Summer 2026—is unrealistic.

                                                        5
                             ii.   Outcome-Determinative Provisions Must Be in a Filed Tariff, and
                                  Subject to Commission Review Before Supporting Financially
                                  Binding Penalties

           SPP’s “rule-of-reason” argument is weak. SPP analogizes caselaw to characterize the

relevant inputs as “implementation details.”12 But SPP also repeatedly concedes that it is willing

to incorporate the Business Practice provisions into the Tariff through a compliance filing. That

concession undermines SPP’s own defense: if these provisions can be placed in the Tariff, they

should be placed there before financially binding obligations take effect.

           Furthermore, SPP’s offer of future compliance filings does not cure the problem. OG&E

cannot begin the multi-year process of securing state regulatory approvals, revising retail tariffs,

re-enrolling customers, and procuring replacement capacity until it knows the final rules under

which compliance will be measured—and those rules will not be final until a compliance filing is

submitted, reviewed, potentially protested, and accepted by the Commission. If the key provisions

remain subject to a pending compliance filing at the time the PDA becomes financially binding,

OG&E will be exposed to deficiency payments under a framework whose terms have not yet been

codified or subject to meaningful review.

           SPP also admits that “[t]he phrase ‘actual Peak Demand’ is not defined,” and asks the

Commission to accept its interpretation, which includes forecasted inputs—thereby reading a

forecasting concept into a term meant to capture observed demand.13 SPP further concedes that the

Business Practices contain no express mechanism for accepting or rejecting an LRE’s weather

normalization methodology; SPP’s only articulated standard is “replicability,” described in




12
  Deficiency Response at 12–16, 30–32 (citing Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp., 184 FERC ¶ 61,207 (2023); Sw. Power
Pool, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,058 (2025); Hecate Energy Greene Cnty. 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307 (D.C. Cir. 2023);
PacifiCorp, 192 FERC ¶ 61,197 (2025)).
13
     Deficiency Response at 17.

                                                      6
 stakeholder meetings, but not set forth in any governing document.14 The instability of the extra-

tariff framework is further demonstrated by the temporary 2,298.5 MW cap on Non-Registered

Demand Response Programs, which SPP revised from 2,152 MW after discovering a forecasting

error before the cap had even taken effect.15

            Finally, SPP concedes that the Tariff contains no formal mechanism for communicating

“additional adjustments” to Post-Season Net Peak Demand, relying instead on communications

that will occur “organically” through existing posting and invoicing.16 Neither posting nor

invoicing provides advance notice of the adjustments on which deficiency payments will be based

before those penalties are assessed. These are outcome-determinative provisions, not mere

implementation details, and they must be subject to Commission review and codified in the filed

Tariff before they can support financially binding penalties.

            The defect is not merely that SPP’s rules are incomplete; it is that SPP seeks authority to

impose financially binding deficiency payments before the governing standards are finalized.

Under SPP’s approach, LREs could incur penalties under requirements that remain uncodified,

undefined, or subject to future revision. The Commission should require SPP first to establish the

complete governing framework in the filed Tariff and only then determine whether that framework

can lawfully support binding compliance obligations.

                           iii.   SPP’s Proposal is Unduly Discriminatory

            SPP’s Proposal remains unduly discriminatory. Under the temporary load modifier cap, an

LRE that adheres to its 2025 Workbook forecast is assessed deficiency payments based on its Pre-

Season Requirement, while an LRE that exceeds its forecasted amount faces assessments based on


14
     Id. at 20.
15
     Id. at 31.
16
     Id. at 26.

                                                     7
 its full Resource Adequacy Requirement. SPP contends that this structure is not discriminatory

because LREs have the “option” to remain within the cap. That purported option is illusory for

LREs such as OG&E whose state-approved demand response programs require regulatory

modifications before they can be changed. OG&E cannot exercise the option to remain within the

cap without first completing state proceedings, revising approved tariffs and program terms, and

educating and re-enrolling customers. Treating the resulting inability to remain within the cap as

an election by OG&E improperly converts regulatory constraints outside OG&E’s control into

enhanced deficiency-payment exposure.

            The PDA increasingly resembles a penalty on forecast variance. Economic growth,

customer additions, electrification, or weather variations may all increase PDA exposure even

where reliability is fully maintained. SPP has failed to explain why forecasting errors should form

the basis for a new penalty construct.

                           iv.    The Implementation Timeline Remains Problematic

            SPP’s stakeholder process does not cure the Proposal’s substantive defects. SPP shifted its

requested effective date from January 1, 2027 to June 1, 2027—only a five-month delay—even

while acknowledging that “a number of LREs indicated that implementation in 2027 would be

impossible due to regulatory constructs and contracts.”17 SPP’s response expressly quotes

OG&E’s stakeholder comments explaining that compliance would require state regulatory filings

and approvals, customer education and subscription, and potentially additional capacity

procurement.18 A five-month cushion is wholly inadequate to complete those steps, particularly

where SPP has acknowledged that some LREs face potentially impossible 2027 timelines.



17
     Id. at 5.
18
     Id. at n. 23.

                                                     8
            Furthermore, SPP’s proposed Business Practice 8100, Section 2.2 would require that LREs

“notify SPP the Demand Response or RRDRP category for the upcoming Summer Season” by

September 1, 2027.19 If the Proposal is effective for Summer 2028, OG&E would have to provide

some level of update to SPP by September 1, 2027. That would be both before the November 1,

2027 market registration date, and before regulatory tariff updates and customer agreements could

be completed. Furthermore, the proposed Business Practice Manual lacks sufficient detail on the

means of notification, requiring that LREs “notify” SPP of Demand Response resources, but

without further definition of the method for notification or the level of detail required.20 Internal

stakeholder approval cannot substitute for a lawful, sufficiently specified filed rate or cure the

practical impossibility of compliance on SPP’s proposed schedule.

                       B. SPP’s Proposal Disproportionately Impacts OG&E and Unjustly
                          Discounts OG&E’s Large, State-Approved Demand Response Program

                            i.       OG&E Has Made Substantial Investments in Demand Response

           SPP’s Proposal imposes a disproportionate burden on OG&E as the LRE with the largest

amount of affected Demand Response in the SPP footprint, and thereby the greatest deficiency

payment exposure, as well as the most enrolled demand response customers, and the most

extensive state-tariff dependencies.21 OG&E has made substantial, state-approved investments in

demand response, operating a comprehensive, large-scale Demand Response Program that benefits

both the wholesale market and the reliability of the grid. Specifically, OG&E’s 2025–2029 demand

program plan projects approximately 100,000 kW (100 MW) of Business Demand Response

impact by 2029 and allocates approximately $26.3 million in total Business Demand Response


19
     Deficiency Response, Attachment 1 at 7.
20
     Id.
21
  OG&E’s demand response program is embedded in state-regulated retail tariffs approved by the Oklahoma
Corporation Commission.

                                                    9
 program costs over the planning cycle.22 In addition, OG&E’s Business Demand Response

program provides approximately 21 MW of measured and verified load reduction.23 OG&E’s

Demand Response Program enables OG&E to meet its capacity obligations, shave peak loads, and

support the grid during scarcity conditions—precisely the results that SPP’s Proposal purports to

encourage.

           OG&E’s demand response investments were neither speculative nor provisional. They

were developed through formal regulatory proceedings, approved by state regulators, funded by

customers, and implemented over many years in reliance on the governing regulatory framework.

SPP’s Proposal would substantially diminish the capacity value of those state-approved

investments while requiring utilities—and ultimately their customers—to incur additional costs to

replace the capacity value lost under SPP’s revised accreditation methodology. The Proposal thus

would impair established reliance interests and impose duplicative costs without a demonstrated

showing that the resulting reliability benefits justify those consequences.

           The following table summarizes the performance of OG&E’s Load Reduction Test

Program from 2022 through 2026, demonstrating the consistent success of these programs:

         Despite OG&E’s strong track record, SPP’s Proposal would discount a significant portion

of this investment by offering incentives for participation in other types of demand response,

making it less likely that OG&E’s currently committed resources would continue participating in

the “load modifier” category of demand response, creating a substantial obligation for OG&E to

procure additional, costly generation resources in an unreasonable timeframe. Specifically, over

100 MW of OG&E’s current load reduction programs are unlikely to be captured under SPP’s

Proposal.24 SPP’s Proposal would devalue resources that have already demonstrated their

effectiveness while steering LREs to pursue alternate compliance pathways that may be costlier,

less certain, and less proven. The Commission should be reluctant to undermine successful state-




24
   Moreover, many current demand response customers enrolled in OG&E’s programs with the understanding that
they would be called upon only during emergency conditions. Under SPP’s Proposal, all such participants would need
to be available more frequently, fundamentally altering the terms of their participation. For example, certain gas
companies currently enrolled in OG&E’s programs cannot be dispatched during winter months and would be unlikely
to re-enroll under the new requirements.

                                                       11
 approved demand response investments, absent compelling evidence that doing so will materially

improve reliability.

        The new accreditation, registration, testing, Firm Service Level, and four-hour-capability

requirements contained in SPP’s Proposal would force OG&E to redesign or curtail state-approved

programs, disrupting existing customer enrollments and incentive structures. Meeting a financially

binding 2028 obligation would require, at minimum: (1) modifying Oklahoma (and, as applicable,

Arkansas) retail tariffs; (2) making state regulatory filings and obtaining the requisite approvals;

(3) re-educating and re-subscribing customers under new program terms; (4) potentially procuring

additional capacity or generation resources that cannot be constructed on this accelerated schedule;

and (5) re-tooling dispatch and measurement systems to comply with SPP’s new protocols.25

Forcing compliance on SPP’s proposed timeline would cause OG&E to suffer an artificially

manufactured capacity shortfall. Such an unjust result further supports extending compliance with

SPP’s Proposal, if ultimately granted, to the 2033 Summer Season to provide the requisite time for

OG&E to complete these regulatory approvals, customer transitions, system modifications, and

replacement-resource development.

        OG&E’s concerns are corroborated by SPP’s MMU, which concluded that “SPP will have

insufficiently defined inputs and constraints” for accrediting Demand Response Resources and

Reliability-Required Demand Response Programs, and that the framework “lacks the detail

required to ensure a reasonable degree of accuracy and consistent outcomes.”26 SPP’s proposed

demand response accreditation and PDA framework delegates critical determinations to individual


25
   Additional implementation considerations requiring lead time include: expanded customer outreach and education;
integration of new SPP-directed notification protocols, which may require significant technology modifications;
adaptation to SPP’s proposed more immediate performance measurement framework (as compared to OG&E’s current
five-year average methodology); and completion of audit procedures with SPP.
26
 Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Protest of Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit, Docket No. ER26-2249-000 (filed
May 8, 2026) (“MMU Protest”).

                                                       12
 LREs—including baseline load measurement, capability testing conditions, firm service level

calculations, and weather normalization methodologies—with minimal oversight, verification, or

enforceable standards. The Oklahoma Corporation Commission has echoed these concerns.27

Before OG&E can redesign customer programs, revise state-approved tariffs, procure replacement

capacity, or commit customer funds, it must understand how demand response resources will

actually be measured, tested, accredited, and valued. The current Proposal provides insufficient

certainty on these foundational issues.

        The MMU’s findings confirm that the lack of specificity is not merely an implementation

concern unique to OG&E; it is a market-design defect that prevents consistent application across

LREs. Without filed, enforceable standards governing the inputs used to determine accreditation

and deficiency payments, similarly situated LREs could be treated differently, SPP’s

determinations would be difficult to test or challenge, and neither the Commission nor market

participants could assess in advance whether resulting charges are just and reasonable. This defect

leaves OG&E unable to determine which existing resources will retain value, how much

replacement capacity will be required, or which investments would be prudent.

        SPP’s Deficiency Response further confirms the uncertainty surrounding weather

normalization. As mentioned above, SPP states it will “accept or reject” an LRE’s submitted

methodology, but concedes there is no express mechanism in the Business Practices for doing so.28

SPP’s sole articulated standard—that a methodology must be “replicable,” meaning SPP staff can

duplicate the results—was described only in stakeholder meetings, not codified in any governing



27
  See Comments of Commissioner Kim David of the Oklahoma Corporation Commission in opposition to Southwest
Power Pool Inc.'s Peak Demand Assessment and Demand Response Proposal, Docket No. ER26-2249 (filed Oct. 9,
2026).
28
  Deficiency Response at 18-20 (“the Business Practices do not explicitly describe an express mechanism to accept
or reject any given methodology”).

                                                       13
 document.29 This ambiguity is further highlighted by SPP citing the Oklahoma Corporation

Commission’s prior approval of OG&E’s 30-year weather normalization methodology as evidence

that LRE methodologies are subject to external “checks.”30 SPP cannot simultaneously rely on

state-approved methodologies to reassure the Commission that its framework is reasonable, while

retaining unbridled discretion to accept or reject those very same methodologies. OG&E developed

a weather normalization methodology through formal state regulatory proceedings—precisely the

type of rigorous, externally vetted approach SPP invokes as a safeguard. But under the current

framework, OG&E has no basis to determine whether that methodology will satisfy SPP’s

undefined evaluation process, leaving OG&E unable to plan with any certainty around a core input

to the PDA.

                            ii.     SPP’s Proposal Will Increase                 Customer    Costs    Without
                                    Demonstrated Reliability Benefits

            SPP’s Proposal has significant customer affordability implications that receive little

attention in the filing, yet the resulting costs will ultimately be borne by customers. Existing

demand response resources represent some of the most cost-effective resources available to LREs.

OG&E has spent years developing demand response programs that successfully reduce peak

demand, improve reliability, and lower costs for customers. Rather than building upon those

investments, SPP’s Proposal devalues a substantial portion of them,31 and forces utilities to pursue

more expensive replacement alternatives.32




29
     Id. at 20.
30
     Id. at 21 & n.60 (citing OCC Order No. 662059 (Cause No. PUD 201500273)).
31
     Supra Section I.B.i.
32
  For example, OG&E’s 2024 and 2026 Integrated Resource Plans (“IRP”) found that new generation resource costs
increased substantially. In just two years—and before the EO—up-front capex costs across technologies (excluding
nuclear) increased by 60% to 70%.

                                                       14
            These concerns are amplified by current market conditions. Across the SPP footprint,

projected demand growth continues to accelerate while long-term resource adequacy forecasts

reflect increasing capacity constraints.33 Requiring utilities to procure replacement resources on

an accelerated timeline will inevitably place further upward pressure on prices.34 When demand

for accredited capacity grows faster than available supply, customers ultimately bear the resulting

costs.

           Put simply, the most affordable and efficient resource is often the resource that does not

have to be built. Before imposing a framework that may strand existing demand response

investments and require substantial replacement procurement, the Commission should require SPP

to demonstrate that reliability benefits justify the resulting customer costs. SPP has not done so

here.

                          iii.     The Proposal Creates Significant Challenges When Considered
                                   Alongside the EO

           Already facing untenable uncertainty created by SPP’s Proposal, OG&E faces significantly

increased procurement difficulties due to the EO, which prohibits the acquisition and installation

of a broad range of foreign-produced grid equipment including: battery storage, inverters,

transformers, and generators.35 The EO explicitly covers grid-connected inverters, battery storage

systems, certain uninterruptible power supply systems, and associated software, which are

essential to renewable energy and storage projects. The EO calls into question the availability,



33
       SPP,    Resource     Adequacy       Report,     2026       Summer     Season      at   4,     available    at
https://www.spp.org/documents/76932/2026%20spp%20summer%20resource%20adequacy%20report.pdf                     (“By
2031, the East BAA is projected to experience a capacity deficit of 11,188 MW and a reserve margin of approximately
-8%, driven by a projected 28% increase in LRE Net Peak Demand compared to only a 1% increase in accredited
capacity”).
34
  Supra n.32; see also Keith Goldberg, Trump Foreign Equipment Order Perplexes Power Cos., Law360 (Sept. 2,
2026).
35
     See, e.g., EO.

                                                        15
 cost, and delivery timelines of the types of resources that OG&E is considering in response to

changing accreditation requirements. This is especially true given that the EO authorizes the

Department of Energy (“DOE”) to impose conditions on certain equipment acquired or installed

before August 26, 2026, including potential isolation, monitoring, disconnection, replacement, or

removal.36 Moreover, the rules to be promulgated under the EO are not yet available. Even when

they are finalized and published, those rules may be subject to judicial challenge—creating further

uncertainty across the industry.

           Thus, OG&E faces uncertainty on several fronts, regarding both how much of its existing

demand response portfolio will qualify under SPP’s evolving framework, and whether replacement

capacity can be procured in time if that portfolio loses accreditation value. If existing demand

response resources lose accreditation value and replacement generation or capacity cannot be

secured in time, OG&E—and its customers—face a manufactured capacity shortfall and unjust

and unreasonable deficiency-payment exposure.

                     C. If the Commission Ultimately Approves SPP’s Proposal, the 2028
                        Compliance Deadline Should Be Extended to 2033

           Even if the Commission determines that SPP’s Proposal should be approved in some form,

the 2028 compliance deadline should be extended to the 2033 Summer Season. Among other

effects, the EO introduces significantly higher risks in the battery energy storage sector—a critical

component to meeting capacity needs under SPP’s Proposal.37 It is possible that various

components used in utility scale battery storage and other assets could come from a Covered

Foreign Entity that the DOE decides to limit in its rules implementing the EO. OG&E analyzed



36
     Id.
37
  See Brian Martucci, Trump grid order likely to cause energy storage delays, cancellations: BloombergNEF, Utility
Dive (Sept. 1, 2026) (noting that Chinese companies supplied approximately 40% of U.S. inverter volumes in 2025);
see also Keith Goldberg, Trump Foreign Equipment Order Perplexes Power Cos., Law360 (Sept. 2, 2026).

                                                       16
 the potential impacts of the EO and the possible changes necessitated by the Proposal, and found

that a substantial, multi-year delay is necessary.38

         A 2033 implementation period is a measured endpoint that accounts for the time required

to resolve the governing rules, complete state regulatory proceedings, educate and enroll

customers, determine the amount of any replacement capacity, and execute procurement and

construction under the EO’s equipment restrictions. The delay allows OG&E to sequence those

steps, rather than commit customer funds before the accreditation rules and eligible supply options

are known. A shorter period would force overlapping regulatory, customer-program, and

infrastructure decisions that depend on one another and cannot prudently be completed in parallel.

Moreover, major equipment lead time can be up to four years for prime mover and main power

transformer delivery with up to two years of construction following delivery, assuming a gas

turbine combined cycle plant. Solar and/or battery energy storage systems could be developed on

a faster timeline but will bring risks related to highly variable accreditation and the possibility of

low accreditation that, when considered over the life of the asset likely renders them not cost

effective for customers when compared to combustion turbines or combined cycle plants. A five-

year implementation delay would allow the supply side of the market additional time to respond

to rapidly increasing demand, reduce upward pressure on capacity prices, preserve affordability

for customers, and avoid forcing utilities into accelerated procurement decisions during an

unusually uncertain period.


38
   A deferral through the 2033 Summer Season is tied to the sequence of steps OG&E anticipates it would need to
complete, not a generalized request for delay. OG&E would need to obtain definitive Tariff rules and implementing
standards; then evaluate the effect on its existing portfolio; pursue state regulatory approvals and tariff modifications;
re-enroll customers whose business models may be able to meet the requirements of a modified tariff; procure, permit,
construct, test, and place replacement resources in service; and interconnect same to the grid, all while adapting to
some form of anticipated EO-related supply constraints. These activities are sequential, interdependent, and largely
outside OG&E’s unilateral control. Extending the deadline to the 2033 Summer Season provides a reasonable
transition period to complete them without sacrificing reliability or exposing customers to deficiency payments under
an incomplete framework.

                                                           17
            While SPP cites reliability concerns, its analysis does not evaluate the legally relevant

alternative presented here: deferral of the financially binding PDA through the 2033 Summer

Season, coupled with transitional reliability protections and continued reliance on OG&E’s

demonstrated demand response portfolio. Earlier implementation could undermine reliability by

discounting or displacing OG&E’s proven demand response resources before replacement

capacity can be procured and placed in service, a risk heightened by the EO’s restrictions and

resulting supply-chain disruption. A transition through the 2033 Summer Season would preserve

existing reliability resources while allowing OG&E to complete the regulatory approvals,

customer transitions, system modifications, and replacement-resource development necessary to

comply with the final framework. On this record, that transition is not merely administratively

preferable; it is the legally supportable means of avoiding unjust and unreasonable deficiency-

payment exposure without compromising reliability.

           Moreover, this proceeding does not concern load alone; it also concerns the ability to secure

additional capacity. SPP’s capacity position is already projected to face significant constraints.39

If existing demand response resources lose accredited capacity value, OG&E would need sufficient

time to redesign those programs and to procure replacement capacity. Current market and supply-

chain conditions materially constrain both measures. Notably, these issues are outside the control

of OG&E, SPP, or the Commission.

           Given that SPP’s Proposal lacks clarity in its terms, the slim margins in the SPP capacity

market, and the new risks associated with supply-chain disruptions, an extension to the 2033

 Summer Season is not only just and reasonable, but also a necessary accommodation, especially

in light of OG&E’s size and the magnitude of changes required.40

        SPP’s own repeated offer to incorporate Business Practice provisions into the Tariff via

compliance filing confirms that the current framework is not ready to impose financially binding

obligations. No deficiency payments should apply to OG&E until the key provisions governing

the load modifier cap, weather normalization standards, the “additional adjustments”

methodology, and the communication of those adjustments to LREs are codified in the filed rate—

and until OG&E has had adequate time to implement the resulting requirements. That would

necessitate deferring the effective date for penalties until 2033. Conditioning compliance on a

framework that SPP itself acknowledges may require further Tariff filings to complete is neither

just nor reasonable.

        II.      CONCLUSION

        At bottom, SPP asks the Commission to approve a materially incomplete framework that

relies upon questionable assumptions, penalizes forecast variance, devalues successful demand

response investments, and increases customer costs without demonstrating commensurate

reliability benefits. The record does not support SPP’s burden under Section 205 of the FPA.
